result: FTD is the second most prevalent form of early onset dementia, characterized by protein misfolding and aggregation, with clinical phenotypes including behavioral, executive, and language dysfunction without primary amnesia, classified into three variants: BV, SV, and PNFA.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide well-established background information about FTD epidemiology, pathology, and clinical classification, all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These are standard characterizations of FTD that are widely accepted in the field.

result: White matter is involved in FTD pathophysiology, with GM atrophy patterns specific to each variant and widespread WM abnormalities observed across major fiber tracts, with WM changes detectable up to 30 years before symptom onset in mutation carriers.
evaluation: Claims C5-C11 summarize prior literature on GM and WM involvement in FTD, all supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the current study's focus on both GM and WM contributions to FTD pathophysiology.

result: GM and WM alterations are interdependent through Wallerian and retrograde degeneration, and prior studies have related both GM and WM atrophy to specific cognitive aspects in FTD variants.
evaluation: Claims C12-C16 establish the theoretical framework for GM-WM interactions and cite prior work linking structural changes to cognition. All claims are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature.

result: All FTD variants showed extensive WM impairments with reduced FC in major associative fibers, with variant-specific differences in BV (frontal/orbitofrontal), PNFA (left frontal motor areas), and SV (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and FD patterns similar to but less extensive than FC.
evaluation: Claims C21-C26 describe fixel-based analysis results shown in Figures 1-2, with appropriate statistical corrections (age, sex, ICV, FWE). The findings are clearly visualized and the variant-specific patterns align with known FTD pathology. The comparison between FC and FD provides complementary information about WM changes.

result: Structural connectivity analysis revealed variant-specific patterns of reduced connectivity: BV showed bilateral insula-inferior frontal and thalamo-frontal reductions; PNFA showed left hemisphere insula-inferior frontal and precentral-middle frontal reductions; SV showed left thalamo-temporal, orbitofrontal-superior frontal, and intra-temporal reductions.
evaluation: Claims C27-C33 describe structural connectivity results shown in Figure 2d-f, using network-based statistics with appropriate corrections. The findings complement the fixel-based analysis and provide region-specific information about connectivity disruptions in each variant.

result: VBM analysis revealed variant-specific GM atrophy patterns: BV showed widespread bilateral reduction in insula, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal cortex; PNFA showed left-predominant premotor, insula, and prefrontal atrophy; SV showed bilateral temporal and insula atrophy. All variants shared insula atrophy.
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 describe VBM results shown in Figure 3, with appropriate statistical corrections (RFT p<0.01). The findings are consistent with known FTD GM atrophy patterns and the overlay analysis (C37-C39) provides useful information about shared and distinct atrophy patterns.

result: Seed-based analysis from peak GM atrophy regions revealed strong relationships between GM atrophy and reduced FC/FD in major fiber tracts (inferior fronto-occipital, uncinate, superior longitudinal fasciculi), with variant-specific associations for each seed location.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 describe seed-based analysis results shown in Figure 4, demonstrating the relationship between GM atrophy and WM impairment. The analysis appropriately uses peak atrophy locations as seeds and shows both common and variant-specific WM associations.

result: Factor analysis identified three cognitive factors: Factor 1 (semantic processing: naming, category fluency, verbal learning), Factor 2 (executive processing: digit span, trail making, letter fluency), and Factor 3 (verbal fluency). SV patients showed lower semantic and higher executive factor scores compared to BV and PNFA.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 describe factor analysis results shown in Figure 5a-b. The three-factor model was statistically validated (p<0.42), and the factor loadings are interpretable. Group differences in factor scores (C48-C49) are supported by statistical tests, though large within-group variability is noted.

result: The semantic factor was associated with FC in uncinate, inferior fronto-occipital, and inferior longitudinal fasciculi, and with reduced connectivity between left temporal regions and thalamus. The executive factor was associated with FC in superior longitudinal fasciculus, corona radiata, corpus callosum, and aslant tract, and with reduced connectivity between left superior frontal gyrus and other frontal/cortical regions. No relationship was found for the verbal fluency factor.
evaluation: Claims C50-C56 describe relationships between cognitive factors and WM/connectivity measures shown in Figure 5c-d, with appropriate corrections for age, sex, ICV, and multiple comparisons (FWE p<0.05). The findings link specific cognitive domains to anatomically relevant WM tracts and connectivity patterns.

result: For semantic processing, GM volume (39.2%) and FC (32.2%) explained more variance than FD (12.7%). For executive processing, FC (31.7%) explained more variance than GM (18.5%) and FD (18.9%). When included together in models, WM contribution was reduced but not eliminated. FD contribution increased with fiber length (p=0.006), while GM showed a trend for negative relationship with fiber length (p=0.058).
evaluation: Claims C57-C63 describe variance explained and tract-specific analyses shown in Figure 6, with appropriate statistical corrections. The findings demonstrate differential contributions of GM and WM to cognitive domains and reveal a length-dependent relationship for FD. The statistical tests are appropriate and the trend-level finding for GM is appropriately qualified.

result: Semantic symptoms were mainly dependent on short-range WM fiber disruption, while damage to long-range WM fibers was preferentially associated with executive dysfunction, with GM contribution predominant for local processing. The differential contributions of WM and GM on cognition depended on fiber length.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19, C66, C104-C107 represent the main findings of the study, supported by the tract-specific analyses showing length-dependent relationships (C61-C63). The conclusion that short-range connections are dominated by GM while long-range connections show greater WM contribution is supported by the data in Figure 6d, though the GM relationship is only at trend level (p=0.058).

result: All FTD cases showed FD/FC abnormalities across a large WM network connecting frontal and temporal cortices, with WM abnormalities linked to GM atrophy and cognitive decline. The study identified a shared network of WM impairment (uncinate, superior longitudinal, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi, cingulum, corpus callosum) across variants, with variant-specific additional impairments.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65, C67-C70 summarize the overall WM findings and compare them to prior literature. The identification of both shared and variant-specific WM impairments is well-supported by the fixel-based and connectivity analyses (Figures 2-4), and the comparison to prior work (C67-C70) is appropriately cited.

result: One of the largest reductions in structural connectivity was between thalamo-frontal regions, supporting that thalamic atrophy is a prominent feature of FTD common across episodic and genetic mutations.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 describe thalamo-frontal connectivity findings from Figure 2d-f and relate them to prior literature on thalamic involvement in FTD. The finding is supported by the structural connectivity analysis and appropriately contextualized with citations.

result: A common semantic factor explained variance in verbal memory, naming, and categorical fluency across FTD variants, consistent with prior studies showing semantic information contributes to phonological lexical activation. A third factor grouped verbal fluency tests, supporting their dual nature.
evaluation: Claims C74-C76, C80 interpret the factor analysis results and relate them to prior literature on semantic processing and verbal fluency. The interpretations are reasonable and appropriately supported by citations to relevant cognitive neuroscience literature.

result: Evidence was found for relationships between semantic deficits and WM impairment in left uncinate, inferior longitudinal, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi, and between left inferior temporal cortex and thalamus. The findings support the hub model for semantic processing with the anterior temporal pole as a trans-modal hub, and suggest the model could be expanded to include subcortical contributions.
evaluation: Claims C81-C88 interpret the semantic factor findings in the context of the hub model for semantic processing. The data (Figures 5c-d) support the involvement of the proposed tracts, and the interpretation is appropriately grounded in prior literature (C82-C87). The suggestion to expand the hub model to include subcortical contributions (C88) is a reasonable inference from the thalamic connectivity findings.

result: Executive function impairment was associated with disruption of frontal WM tracts (superior longitudinal fasciculus, corona radiata, corpus callosum, aslant tract), with WM contribution increasing with tract length. Reduced WM integrity in large-scale tracts was the major contributor to executive dysfunction in FTD.
evaluation: Claims C89-C96 interpret the executive factor findings and relate them to prior literature on executive function neuroanatomy. The associations with specific tracts (C89) are supported by Figure 5d, the length-dependent relationship (C95) is supported by Figure 6d (p=0.006), and the prior literature on tract functions (C90-C94) is appropriately cited.

result: Large-scale WM tracts are particularly vulnerable to vascular disease and were highly associated with executive dysfunction. The findings highlight the importance of controlling vascular risk factors in FTD patients to avoid potentiating executive dysfunction, though FTD patients are typically younger with less vascular disease, suggesting possible vulnerability to degenerative pathology.
evaluation: Claims C20, C97-C101, C130 make inferences about vascular vulnerability and clinical implications. While the association between long-range tracts and executive function is supported (C95-C96), the connection to vascular vulnerability relies on general knowledge (C20, C97-C98) and the clinical recommendation (C99, C130) is speculative. The alternative explanation (C100-C101) acknowledges uncertainty but remains speculative.

result: The magnitude of GM atrophy was strongly related to WM network impairment, consistent with prior work in AD and FTD. The results support the critical importance of considering both GM and WM alterations for understanding spatially distributed cognitive alterations in neurodegeneration.
evaluation: Claims C102-C103, C108 describe the GM-WM relationship findings (Figure 4) and their implications. The strong relationship between GM atrophy and WM impairment is demonstrated by the seed-based analysis, and the comparison to prior work (C103) is appropriately cited. The conclusion about the importance of multimodal approaches (C108) is a reasonable inference from the findings.

result: Traditional DTI may lead to artifactual findings in neurodegenerative disorders. Novel techniques like constrained spherical deconvolution and FBA have improved dMRI accuracy. FD measures WM microstructure while FC measures macroscopic fiber bundle changes. Both FD and FC were reduced in similar WM regions in FTD, suggesting both fiber atrophy and axonal depletion. This is the first study applying FBA to analyze WM impairments across FTD phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C109-C115 describe the methodological advantages of FBA over traditional DTI and interpret the FD/FC findings. The limitations of DTI (C109) and advantages of newer methods (C110) are appropriately cited. The interpretations of FD and FC (C111-C112) are consistent with the literature (cited to Raffelt et al., 2017). The finding that both metrics were reduced (C114) is supported by Figure 2. The novelty claim (C115) appears reasonable based on the authors' literature review.

result: Most prior studies did not investigate relationships between specific cognitive domains, whole brain WM properties, and structural connectivity. This study provided a more complete picture of specific WM tracts involved in core FTD cognitive impairment using an innovative connection-based framework to quantify simultaneous contributions of WM and GM abnormalities.
evaluation: Claims C116-C118 describe the study's contributions relative to prior work. The assessment of prior literature (C116) appears reasonable, and the study's comprehensive approach (C117-C118) is evident from the multimodal analyses presented. The connection-based framework for disentangling GM and WM contributions is indeed innovative.

result: Study limitations include limited sample size, lack of longitudinal data, lack of genetic/pathological information, multicentric data acquisition (though quality controlled), limited spatial resolution (2.2mm isotropic, the maximum for good SNR), and lack of control for disease duration and symptom severity (which could bias results in this diverse population).
evaluation: Claims C119-C128 acknowledge study limitations. The limitations are appropriately identified and the justifications for methodological choices (e.g., C126 on resolution, C128 on not controlling for disease variables) are reasonable. The acknowledgment of multicentric data with quality control (C121-C122) is appropriate.

result: The results support the importance of WM tract disruption to core cognitive symptoms associated with FTD.
evaluation: Claim C129 is the main conclusion of the study, well-supported by the comprehensive analyses showing relationships between WM metrics and cognitive factors (Figures 5-6), particularly the tract-specific findings demonstrating differential contributions based on fiber length.

result: Data were obtained from FTLDNI, a multicentric longitudinal database. The study included 155 participants (68 CN, 28 BV, 30 PNFA, 26 SV) with cross-sectional DWI passing quality control. Patients were clinically diagnosed by multidisciplinary consensus. MRI acquisition included 65 DWI volumes (60 directions, b=2000) and 3D MPRAGE for GM volume.
evaluation: Claims C131-C137 describe the study sample and data acquisition. The information is clearly stated and appropriately documented with citations for the diagnostic procedures (C133). The sample sizes and acquisition parameters are adequate for the analyses performed.

result: dMRI preprocessing used MRtrix3 and included denoising, Gibbs correction, eddy-current/motion correction, and bias field correction. Response functions were estimated using unsupervised methods. Single-shell 3-tissue CSD was performed to obtain WM FODs and GM/CSF compartments. Images were upsampled to 1.3mm and registered to a study-specific template. A whole brain tractogram was generated and filtered from 20M to 2M tracts.
evaluation: Claims C138-C145 describe dMRI preprocessing and analysis methods, all appropriately cited to relevant methodological papers. The preprocessing pipeline follows current best practices for dMRI analysis. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication.

result: FBA framework was used to compute FD and FC at the fixel level. A fixel refers to a fiber population in a voxel, allowing individual measures for crossing fibers. FD represents intra-axonal microstructural alterations while FC represents macroscopic fiber bundle changes.
evaluation: Claims C146-C150 describe the FBA methodology and interpretation of metrics, appropriately cited to Raffelt et al. papers. The explanation of fixels and the distinction between FD and FC are accurate and important for interpreting the results.

result: Structural connectivity analysis used probabilistic tractography with dynamic seeding to generate 20M tracks, filtered using SIFT. The DKT atlas was used to compute fiber connections between 68 GM regions. The atlas was transformed to diffusion space and corrected by WM FOD amplitude. Connectomes were calculated as fiber counts between region pairs and visualized using BrainNet Viewer.
evaluation: Claims C151-C157 describe structural connectivity methods, all appropriately cited. The methods are standard for structural connectivity analysis and the atlas transformation approach is reasonable. The visual inspection mentioned in the text (not in claims) provides quality control.

result: VBM analysis used SPM12 for tissue segmentation. A study-specific template was created from 30 CN using DARTEL. Individual GM maps were registered to the template, modulated, and filtered (8mm FWHM). ICV was calculated as the sum of GM, WM, and CSF probabilities.
evaluation: Claims C158-C162 describe VBM methods using standard SPM12/DARTEL pipeline. The methods are appropriate and the 8mm smoothing kernel is reasonable for VBM analysis. The ICV calculation method is standard.

result: Maximum likelihood common factor analysis with varimax rotation was used to obtain a parsimonious representation of cognitive scores. A two-factor model was rejected (p<0.05) while a three-factor model was not rejected (p<0.42), providing satisfactory explanation of covariation. Factor scores were calculated using weighted least squares.
evaluation: Claims C163-C165 describe factor analysis methods. The approach is appropriate for reducing dimensionality of cognitive data. The statistical testing of model fit is appropriate, though the p-value for the three-factor model (p<0.42) suggests adequate but not excellent fit. The method is clearly described.

result: Tract of interest analysis selected GM region pairs based on significant connectivity. Streamlines connecting selected regions were extracted and thresholded into binary fixel masks. FC and FD values were averaged in masks. GM volume was calculated as average VBM values of connecting regions. Standardized GM, FC, and FD were used in repeated GLM to obtain prediction estimates adjusted for age, sex, and ICV. Average streamline length was calculated for each tract.
evaluation: Claims C166-C172 describe the tract of interest analysis methods. This innovative approach allows for tract-specific assessment of GM and WM contributions to cognition. The methods are clearly described and the statistical approach (repeated GLM with covariates) is appropriate.

result: Statistical analysis used connectivity-based fixel enhancement for whole brain FBA and network-based statistical enhancement for structural connectivity. Family-wise correction used permutation testing (n=1000). VBM used VoxelStats with random field theory correction (cluster threshold p<0.01). Cognitive analyses were performed in patients only. All models were corrected for age, sex, and ICV.
evaluation: Claims C173-C180 describe statistical methods. The approaches are appropriate for the respective analyses, with proper multiple comparison corrections. The use of permutation testing (n=1000) is adequate. The decision to analyze cognition in patients only (C179) is reasonable given the focus on cognitive impairment.
